q: Which term names a programming approach that organizes a program around objects rather than simply organizing instructions into separate functions?
options: Procedure-oriented programming (POP)
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)
Structured programming
Recursive programming
explanation: OOP organizes a program around objects that have attributes and methods. Procedural and structured programming organize instructions into steps and functions; recursion is a function calling itself.

q: What is a class in Python?
options: A concrete realization of a blueprint that exists in memory as one specific, actual thing of that type
A variable that belongs to one particular object and can differ for every object
A function defined inside an object that describes one of its actions
A user-defined blueprint or template that defines the structure and behavior shared by all objects of that type
explanation: A class is the blueprint. The concrete thing in memory is an object, a per-object variable is an instance attribute, and a function inside a class is a method.

q: What is an object (instance)?
options: A concrete realization of a class; the actual thing existing in memory
The template that defines what all objects of one type share
A special method that runs automatically as soon as a class is defined
A variable defined inside a class and shared by every instance
explanation: A class defines WHAT something is; an object IS the actual thing in memory, created with ClassName(). The shared variable is a class attribute, and __init__ runs when an object is created, not when the class is defined.

q: A variable defined directly inside a class but outside its methods, and generally shared by all instances, is called a(n):
options: Instance attribute
Instance method
Class attribute
Static method
explanation: A class attribute such as school = "University of the Cordilleras" sits in the class body outside any method and is shared. Instance attributes belong to one object and are usually set in __init__ with self.

q: Which term means a variable that belongs to a particular object and can have a different value for every object?
options: Class attribute
Instance attribute
Class method
Local variable of __init__
explanation: Instance attributes, such as self.name, belong to one object. A plain local variable inside __init__ (name = name) disappears after __init__ ends and is not stored on the object.

q: If attributes represent what an object HAS, what do methods represent?
options: What the object DOES: functions defined inside a class that describe its behaviors
What the object IS: the blueprint that defines its structure
Values that describe the object, such as its brand, model, color, year, and speed
The specific instantiation of a class that exists in memory
explanation: Methods are class functions describing actions, such as start engine or brake for a Car. Brand and color are attributes, the blueprint is the class, and the instantiation is an object.

q: Inside an instance method, what does `self` refer to?
options: The class itself, which is shared by all objects of that type
The first value typed inside the call parentheses
The module in which the class is defined
The current object (instance) the method was called on
explanation: In student2.introduce(), self is student2. The class itself is what cls refers to in a class method. Python passes the object automatically, so it is not the first value typed in the call.

q: In a class method, what does the `cls` parameter refer to?
options: The current object (instance) on which the method was called
The most recently created instance of the class
The class itself, similar to how self refers to an object
The value returned by the __init__ method
explanation: cls is the class, so cls.school = new_school changes the class attribute. The current object is self, used in instance methods.

q: Which line correctly creates an object of the class `Student` and stores it in `student1`?
options: `student1 = Student()`
`student1 = Student`
`Student = student1()`
`student1 = new Student()`
explanation: An object is created with the class name followed by parentheses: object_name = ClassName(). Without parentheses, student1 just refers to the class itself; `new` is Java syntax and is invalid in Python.

q: Which expression uses correct dot notation to read the `course` attribute of the object `student1`?
options: `course.student1`
`student1.course`
`student1->course`
`student1[course]`
explanation: Dot notation is object_name.attribute_name. The arrow is C/C++ syntax, and square brackets are for indexing lists and dictionaries.

q: Which class header is valid Python and follows the usual naming convention?
options: `class student_record:`
`def StudentRecord:`
`class StudentRecord:`
`class StudentRecord()`
explanation: Classes are defined with the keyword class, a PascalCase name, and a colon. student_record runs but is not PascalCase, def defines functions, and the header without a colon is a SyntaxError.

q: Which definition correctly creates a class method that changes the class attribute `school`?
options: `@staticmethod` above `def change_school(cls, new_school):` with body `cls.school = new_school`
`@classmethod` above `def change_school(cls):` with body `cls.school = new_school`
No decorator, then `def change_school(cls, new_school):` with body `cls.school = new_school`
`@classmethod` above `def change_school(cls, new_school):` with body `cls.school = new_school`
explanation: A class method needs the @classmethod decorator and cls as its first parameter. @staticmethod passes no cls, so Student.change_school("UB") puts "UB" into cls and new_school is missing (TypeError). Without new_school as a parameter, the call passes one value too many (TypeError), and without the decorator "UB" lands in cls and new_school is missing (TypeError).

q: What does Python create in memory when it runs a class definition such as `class Student:`?
options: A class object; no instance exists until `Student()` is called
One instance of Student, stored automatically in a variable named student
Nothing; memory is used only when the first method of the class runs
One instance for each attribute written inside the class body
explanation: Defining a class creates a class object in memory, not an instance. Instances are created only by calling the class, as in student1 = Student().

q: `Student` has `def __init__(self, name, age, course)`. When `student1 = Student("Juan", 20, "BSIT")` runs, in what order do these happen?
options: student1 is assigned first; then __init__ must be called manually to set the attributes
A new Student object is created; __init__ runs automatically with that object as self; self.name, self.age and self.course are assigned; the object is stored in student1
__init__ stores the values on the class; then a new object is created that copies them
The attributes are assigned to student1 first; then the Student object is created; then __init__ runs automatically and returns it
explanation: __init__ runs automatically right after the new object is created, receives it as self, stores the passed values as instance attributes, and then the finished object is assigned to the variable.

q: What is the correct order for using a class in a program?
options: Create an object with ClassName(), then define the class with the class keyword, then access its attributes and methods with dot notation
Access attributes with dot notation, define the class, then create an object with ClassName()
Define the class, access attributes with object_name.attribute_name, then create the object with ClassName()
Define the class with the class keyword, create an object with ClassName(), then access its attributes and methods with dot notation
explanation: The class must exist before an object can be created from it, and the object must exist before object_name.attribute_name can be read. Any other order raises a NameError.

q: When Python evaluates `student1.school`, in what order does it look for the attribute?
options: First in the class Student, then in the object student1
Only in the class Student, because objects cannot hold their own attributes
First in the object student1's own attributes, then in the class Student
First in the parameters of __init__, then in the object student1
explanation: Python checks the object first, so an instance attribute created by student1.school = "UC" hides the class attribute for that object. If the object has none, the class attribute is used.

q: A method `update_grade` must change an object's grade to a value given in the call. In what order are its parameters written?
options: `def update_grade(new_grade, self):`
`def update_grade(self, new_grade):`
`def update_grade(new_grade):`
`def update_grade(cls, new_grade):`
explanation: An instance method takes self first, then any additional parameters. Putting self last puts the object into new_grade; leaving out self gives a TypeError; cls is for class methods with @classmethod.

q: Which statement about `self` is NOT true?
options: self is a reserved Python keyword, so no other name can be used in its place
self refers to the current instance of the class
self lets an object access its own attributes and methods
Python passes self automatically as the first argument when a method is called through an object
explanation: self is not a reserved keyword; it is a naming convention. It can technically be replaced with another name, but doing so is strongly discouraged.

q: Which description of a method type is mismatched?
options: Instance method: first parameter self, no decorator
Class method: first parameter cls, decorator @classmethod
Static method: first parameter cls, decorator @staticmethod
Class method: main purpose is to access or modify class attributes
explanation: A static method receives neither self nor cls automatically; only the class method takes cls. The other three rows match the comparison of method types.

q: Which statement comparing class attributes and instance attributes is NOT true?
options: Class attributes are defined directly inside the class, outside its methods
Instance attributes are usually defined inside __init__() using self
Class attributes are commonly accessed through the class name rather than through one object
Instance attributes are shared among all objects of the class unless overridden
explanation: Sharing among instances unless overridden describes class attributes. Instance attributes belong to individual objects and are accessed through an object.

q: Which statement about the `__init__()` method is NOT true?
options: It must be called manually after each object is created in order to set its attributes
It runs automatically whenever a new object is created
It is commonly used to initialize an object's instance attributes
Without it, attributes must be assigned separately after each object has been created
explanation: __init__ is the constructor: Python calls it automatically when ClassName(...) runs. Without __init__, you create the object first and then assign student1.name = ... and so on separately.

q: What does this code print?
code:
class Student:
    school = "UB"
s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
s1.school = "UC"
Student.school = "SLU"
s3 = Student()
print(s1.school, s2.school, s3.school)
options: `SLU SLU SLU`
`UC UB SLU`
`UC UC SLU`
`UC SLU SLU`
explanation: s1.school = "UC" creates an instance attribute on s1 only. Student.school = "SLU" changes the class attribute, which s2 and s3 read because they have no own school. s1 keeps its own value UC.

q: What does this code print?
code:
class Pet:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age
a = Pet("Bantay", 3)
b = Pet("Muning", 5)
a.age = b.age + 1
print(a.name, a.age, b.age)
options: `Bantay 6 5`
`Bantay 4 5`
`Bantay 6 6`
`Muning 6 5`
explanation: Each object has its own instance attributes. b.age is 5, so a.age becomes 5 + 1 = 6. Changing a.age does not change b.age, which stays 5.

q: This code stops with an error. Which line raises it, and why?
options: `d = Dog("Brownie")`, because __init__ has two parameters (self and name) but only one argument was given
`self.name = name`, because name is not defined inside __init__
`d.bark()`, because bark has no self parameter but Python passes the object automatically (TypeError)
`print("Woof")`, because a method cannot call print
explanation: Dog("Brownie") is correct: self is passed automatically and "Brownie" goes to name. d.bark() passes d as the first argument, but def bark(): accepts none, giving TypeError: bark() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given. Fix: def bark(self):.

q: What happens when this code runs?
code:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, pages):
        title = title
        self.pages = pages
b = Book("Noli", 300)
print(b.pages)
print(b.title)
options: It prints Noli, then 300
It prints 300, then raises an AttributeError because the title was never stored with self.title
It raises an AttributeError before printing anything
It prints 300, then prints None, because a title that was never stored defaults to None
explanation: self.pages = pages stores pages, so print(b.pages) shows 300. title = title only reassigns a local variable inside __init__, so the object has no title attribute and print(b.title) raises an AttributeError. Fix: self.title = title.

24, then 12, then 12
